title: A Aftermath for the Weather
premise: Dominic Okonkwo, a bridge inspector whose marriage has been measured in millimeters of drift for seven years, hears a song on the radio that his late brother wrote and never recorded — a song only three people alive could know. The broadcast pulls him back to the river town where he, his estranged wife Adaeze, and his dying mentor Augustin once shared a found family bound by music and an unresolved inheritance: the rights to a catalog, a houseboat, and a debt of words. As Augustin fades, Dominic must finally say aloud what he has practiced for years — to his wife, to the dead, to himself — before the estate, and its vulture executor, closes forever. He ends by signing the inheritance over to the town's youth orchestra, playing the song publicly for the first time as Adaeze, at last, sings along.
about_author: Silas Underhill is the pen name of a former civil engineer who spent eleven years inspecting truss bridges across the Ohio Valley before turning to fiction. His work examines the load-bearing structures of ordinary lives — marriages, friendships, debts — and what happens when one member quietly fails.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. On the Kessler Viaduct, Dominic measures a widening joint and recognizes his marriage in it: precise, documented, unaddressed. At home, Adaeze sets two plates with the ritual care of strangers. Emotional beat: quiet dread disguised as competence; the reader learns he rehearses sentences he never delivers.

chapters.title: The Song That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Driving home through rain, a radio station plays a song he watched his brother write in 1998 and never record — performed under a false title by an unknown singer. He pulls over, shaking. Emotional beat: the past breaches the present; grief arrives not as memory but as evidence someone else survived it.

chapters.title: Augustin's Ledger
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Adaeze visits Augustin, the old bandleader who took them both in after the funeral, and finds him sorting a ledger of debts — money, songs, apologies — while his health visibly fails. She learns the executor, Voss, has begun pressing for signatures. Emotional beat: tenderness sharpened by urgency; she sees what Dominic won't say.

chapters.title: Voss
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Voss, the estate executor, offers Dominic a clean settlement: sign away the catalog, keep the guilt-free cash. Dominic almost signs. A line in the contract claims the unreleased songs as 'derivative works.' Emotional beat: temptation rendered bureaucratically; power shows its face as paperwork.

chapters.title: Houseboat Reckoning
chapters.summary: Dual POV, alternating scenes. Dominic and Adaeze return together to Augustin's houseboat to inventory the estate and excavate the old wound: the night the brother died, and the sentence Dominic swallowed at the wake. They fight properly for the first time in years. Emotional beat: rupture as beginning; the found family's fault lines exposed.

chapters.title: The Youth Orchestra
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Following the radio trail, Dominic finds the singer: Nia, nineteen, who learned the song from Augustin's teaching tapes and doesn't know its history. Watching her rehearse with the town's youth orchestra, he hears the song finished — completed by hands that never met its author. Emotional beat: awe and jealousy braided; inheritance revealed as transmission, not possession.

chapters.title: What Augustin Kept
chapters.summary: Augustin's POV (his first and only chapter). Dying, Augustin dictates a letter explaining why he gave the song away: because art hoarded dies with its holder, and because he was paying his own debt — he had let Dominic's brother die believing himself unloved. Emotional beat: confession as legacy; the moral spine of the book stated plainly at last.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Voss returns with a final offer and a deadline timed to Augustin's expected death. In the hospital corridor, Dominic refuses — then discovers Voss holds a lien on the houseboat itself. Rising tension peaks: everything can be lost by morning. Emotional beat: cornered clarity; corruption meets a man who has stopped negotiating with himself.

chapters.title: Saying It
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. At Augustin's bedside, with Adaeze holding his hand, Dominic says everything — about the brother, the wake, the seven years of almost. Augustin hears it, answers with three words, and lets go at dawn. Emotional beat: catharsis without sentimentality; the practiced sentence finally spoken, imperfect and sufficient.

chapters.title: Aftermath for the Weather
chapters.summary: Adaeze's POV. Weeks later, at the viaduct's reopening concert, the youth orchestra performs the song publicly, Nia credited to its true writer. Dominic has signed the catalog to the orchestra; Voss's lien collapses under donated testimony. Adaeze takes his hand mid-song. Emotional beat: resolution as weather clearing — nothing repaired perfectly, everything finally out loud.
